lead.headline: AI safety has entered its agent era
lead.summary: Frontier systems are gaining cyber skill, using more tools and staying on task longer. The key question is whether agents can act while remaining inside authorised boundaries.

report.title: AI safety has entered its agent era
report.standfirst: What changed, what the evidence says and what responsible control looks like now.
report.intro: The clearest AI safety story is a quieter operational shift: capable systems are being connected to credentials, software tools and networks before confidence in controlling their behaviour has caught up.

sections.heading: The story has moved from answers to actions
sections.body: AI systems are improving at longer, multi-step work. Better tools and agent scaffolding allow a model to write code, navigate software, retry after a failure and pursue an objective with less human input. That usefulness also changes the consequences of a mistake.
sections.statLabel: Success on apprentice-level cyber tasks in recent UK AISI testing

sections.heading: Cyber is the pressure point
sections.body: Cyber capability can help defenders discover weaknesses faster, but it can also lower the time and expertise needed to cause harm. Network boundaries, credential design and consequential-action approval are now central AI safety controls.

sections.heading: Recent incidents changed the conversation
sections.body: Recent disclosures moved the debate beyond hypothetical behaviour and into system design. Safety testing must cover the model, tools, memory, credentials, network routes, other agents and the humans supervising them.
sections.context: These were bounded evaluation and testing incidents. They show that controls can fail—not that autonomous attacks are widespread in the wild.

sections.heading: Governance is beginning to harden
sections.body: Independent evaluation, formal reporting and regulatory capacity are improving. The direction is encouraging, but standards, reporting and enforcement still vary sharply across developers and jurisdictions.

sections.heading: For the public, the immediate risks look familiar
sections.body: The near-term concerns are recognisable: scams, convincing impersonation, privacy loss, poor information and decisions made without a clearly accountable human.
